meta.title: Deadlines to file an employment-discrimination charge: the federal EEOC limit and each state agency's own limit
meta.attribution: Source: Probative, Deadlines to file an employment-discrimination charge: the federal EEOC limit and each state agency's own limit, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23782861, licensed CC BY 4.0.

summary: How long a worker has to file a charge of employment discrimination: the EEOC's 180-day limit and its 300-day extension, and the limit each covered state's own statute sets for its civil-rights agency. One row per rule, with the statute citation, the official document's URL and the verbatim quote (25 words or fewer) that carries the number.

records.text: United States: time to file a federal charge of discrimination: 180 calendar days (EEOC, Time Limits For Filing A Charge). The EEOC extends this to 300 calendar days when a state or local agency enforces a law against discrimination on the same basis.
records.cite: EEOC, Time Limits For Filing A Charge
records.quote: In general, you need to file a charge within 180 calendar days from the day the discrimination took place.
records.document: Time Limits For Filing A Charge (EEOC)

sources.label: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: Time Limits For Filing A Charge (EEOC)

source.release: Time Limits For Filing A Charge (EEOC)
source.file: Time Limits For Filing A Charge (EEOC)

records.note: The EEOC extends this to 300 calendar days when a state or local agency enforces a law against discrimination on the same basis.

records.text: United States: extended time to file a federal charge where a state or local agency enforces a law on the same basis: 300 calendar days (EEOC, Time Limits For Filing A Charge). For age discrimination the extension applies only where a state law and a state agency cover age.
records.cite: EEOC, Time Limits For Filing A Charge
records.quote: extended to 300 calendar days if a state or local agency enforces a law that prohibits employment discrimination on the same basis
